standard.title: Significant Individuals and Groups Promoting Industrial Revolution Ideas
standard.description: the role of a significant individual or group such as agricultural and factory workers, inventors and entrepreneurs, landowners, politicians and religious groups in promoting and enacting some of the ideas that emerged during the Industrial Revolution
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the ideas that emerged during the Industrial Revolution (AC9HH9K17) and understand the ideological landscape of the period. They understand how conditions generated ideas. This descriptor asks them to examine the human agency behind those ideas — how specific individuals and groups promoted and enacted ideological change.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the role of a significant individual or group in promoting and enacting ideas that emerged during the Industrial Revolution.

nodes.label: Responses to specific ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how different groups and individuals responded to the key ideas of the Industrial Revolution period, including both support and opposition.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one group or type of individual responded to one idea that emerged during the Industrial Revolution.
nodes.typical_width: Explain responses to particular ideas — including: how religious groups responded to Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859); how workers responded to capitalism and socialism; how industrialists responded to reform proposals; how governments responded to Chartism; explaining why the same idea generated different responses in different groups.
wider: Examine the scientific and religious debate over Darwin's theory of evolution as a case study in how a new idea disrupted established frameworks — tracing the range of responses from outright rejection to accommodation to enthusiastic embrace

Investigate how working-class communities developed their own intellectual and cultural life (mechanics' institutes, reading rooms, Chartist newspapers) as a response to capitalism — examining workers as active agents of ideas, not only recipients of others' ideologies

response_modes.reason: Using multiple idea-response pairings (Darwin + religion; capitalism + workers; Chartism + government) shows that response to ideas is not uniform — the same idea generates different responses depending on social position and prior commitments.

success_criteria: Explains how at least two different groups responded to an idea of the period, showing why responses differed
Identifies at least one factor (social position, religious belief, economic interest) that shaped how a group responded to an idea

nodes.label: Role of a significant individual or group in promoting an idea
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the role played by one significant individual or group in promoting a key idea of the Industrial Revolution period, assessing the effectiveness of their contribution.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the role of one significant individual or group in promoting an idea that emerged during the Industrial Revolution.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the role played by an individual or group in promoting a key idea — including: Adam Smith and entrepreneurs promoting capitalism; Florence Nightingale promoting healthcare reform and women's rights; Pope Leo XIII promoting workers' rights in capitalist economies (Rerum Novarum); Chartist William Cuffay in Tasmania or British Chartists on Australian goldfields; explain how these individuals or groups used their position, networks, and resources to advance their ideas.
wider: Investigate the role of William Cuffay — a Black British Chartist leader transported to Tasmania — examining both his leadership within the Chartist movement and what his biography reveals about the intersections of race, class, and political activism in the industrial period

Examine British Chartists on the Victorian goldfields as an example of how industrial-era ideas and activists moved through imperial networks — assessing how Chartist ideas influenced early Australian democratic culture

Compare two individuals who promoted opposing ideas in response to the same conditions (e.g. Adam Smith promoting free-market capitalism vs Robert Owen promoting cooperative socialism) — assessing the influence of each on subsequent social development

response_modes.reason: The range of individuals in the elaborations — from capitalist theorists to workers' advocates, from religious reformers to activists transported to Australia — is deliberately diverse. Widening to include less-familiar figures (Cuffay, Chartists in Australia) is especially valuable.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The figures in this descriptor include some who are rarely studied — William Cuffay (a Black Chartist leader), British Chartists in colonial Australia — whose stories both enrich the historical picture and challenge assumptions about who was involved in industrial-era reform. These are pedagogically significant as examples of underrepresented voices in history.
success_criteria: Investigates the role of at least one significant individual or group in promoting an industrial-era idea
Explains how that individual or group used their particular resources or position to advance their ideas
